Source: National Laboratory of the Rockies The AMD concept was conceived for the city of Houston through collaborative discussions with officials from the city of Houston and Houston METRO, as depicted in Figure 4. Each high- density urban district within a 4-mile radius at the center of the urban core of Houston yields substantial and significant intradistrict trip demand synonymous with the concept of AMDs, for which AV technologies may provide a tractable mobility solution to increase accessibility while addressing traffic and parking congestion. Further, the proximity of five major urban districts within a 4-mile radius calls for efficient regional connections. The FMLM service of an AMD AV fleet would provide connectivity to intermodal hubs for this purpose as well as access to other regional transit services. This enhances not only mobility between AMDs but also connectivity and accessibility to people and locations outside the urban core. In the case of Houston, this also allows for connections to the future high-speed rail terminal that is planned at the northwest edge of the urban core. Further, multiple high-density AMDs in proximity, as is the case for the urban core of Houston, may also justify the use of AV fleet services between mobility hubs for interdistrict connectivity. In addition, the AMD concept supports the emphasis from the city of Houston and Houston METRO of expanding the service area to serve communities that have historically not been well served.
